labs.Anthropic: Thelma Newton was two years and nine months old. She had four teeth at the top, six at the bottom, a fringe her mother had cut herself, and a red woollen coat with five buttons down the front. Four of the buttons were ordinary. They were black and round, with four holes in the middle, and they did their job without fuss. The fifth button, the top one, was not ordinary at all. The top button was made of mother-of-pearl. It had come off a cardigan that belonged to Thelma's great-grandmother, who had worn it to dances in the days when people still danced in the village hall on Saturday nights. When Thelma's mother sewed it onto the red coat, she held it up to the kitchen window so that Thelma could see the light move across it, pink and silver and a faint, secret green, like the inside of a shell or the surface of a puddle with petrol in it. "Moon," said Thelma, who was very sure about things. So it was called Moon from then on. Thelma did not let anyone else do up Moon. She did the bottom four buttons on her own, and that took a long time, with her tongue sticking out of the corner of her mouth. Moon she did last, with great ceremony, and when it was done she patted it twice, once to say hello and once to say well done. Every morning, while her mother went to work at the chemist's in town, Thelma's grandad walked her down the lane to the duck pond and back. Grandad walked slowly because of his knees, and Thelma walked slowly because there was a great deal to look at, so the arrangement suited both of them. They looked at snails. They looked at a crisp packet caught in the hedge. They looked at the Albrights' cat, who looked back at them with contempt. And every morning they passed Mister Edwards's field. Mister Edwards's field was large and muddy and had a five-bar gate set into the hedge beside the lane. In it lived a horse. The horse was called Pudding. This was the only soft thing about him. Pudding was a shire horse, or mostly a shire horse, with something else mixed in that nobody could identify and nobody liked to guess at. He was the colour of wet coal. His feet were the size of dustbin lids and covered in long, dirty white hair, like the feet of a giant who had stopped caring about his appearance. His head was as long as Thelma was tall.

Night had long arrived when Mara locked up her bakery and dropped off a warm roll for the silent violinist who was always playing under the station’s clock, like she did every night. They smiled at each other. Mara wanted to say something, but the words stuck in her throat. She rushed off to board the last train of the night. One Tuesday night, the violinist was missing. Instead, there lay an envelope beneath the clock. Mara picked it up and inside was a ticket to a midnight conservation concert with an invitation letter. “Come hear the music that your bread has sustained”, it wrote. Mara thought about the letter all week.

It is midnight in the industrial city of Bellweather. The city is filled with soot and has not seen sunlight in eighteen years due to it being outlawed by the emperor. The people of the city live in constant fear of the oppressive regime that holds a monopoly over light and power. Most people work in factories with dangerous conditions and poor pay. If they lose a limb at work, they aren’t able to afford getting a mechanical replacement like the soldiers in the imperial army. At night, the soldiers and the emperor’s mechanical ravens patrol the streets to enforce curfew on the citizens.

Mara stands before the Helix Corporation tower. Despite the pouring rain, she doesn’t have time to worry about herself getting drenched. Somewhere among these 100 floors, she needs to reclaim her brother Tomas’s refrigerated memories. Five years ago, Mara was diagnosed with cancer. She had no choice but to use Tomas’s memories as collateral for a medical loan. Without steady income, there was no way for her to pay it back in time. Under legal terms, Helix confiscated the memories. One night when Mara tried to drink away her sorrows at the bar, a man in white suit approached her and introduced himself as Saint the illicit broker. He consoled her and gave her a key.

The sun rises and another peaceful day in 1755 starts. The red roofs of beautiful buildings at downtown Lisbon are shining and people gather around the church to enjoy a fresh new day. “Look at that clear sky, it’s so spacious that it feels like it’s going to absorb me”, says Inês Vale. Her brother Tomás says, “Yeah, it is truly marvelous!” Inês and Tomás are carrying candles to their church, edging their way through the bustling streets.

The one small sapling in Pip’s garden had died overnight. Pip touched the drooping leaves and sighed. The village of Willowmere was known for its flourishing gardens of colorful, singing flowers. Pip’s patch of barren land was the exception. He spent hours in his garden every day to no avail. He was ready to give up hope. Then, one moonlit night, he met Sprout. Sprout was a shivering green seed with a silver cap who had been carried by the wind to Pip’s window. “There now,” Pip said. “That should be better, right?” Pip had gently placed Sprout in his garden soil under an oven-warmed mitten. “I hope you do not find my garden to be too lonely,” Pip said.

“You could feel the tension in the air. Dark, ominous clouds above. I actually loved thunderstorms, used to find the weather exciting. One moment, there’s quiet. Even the birds knew. In a split second, it’s raining so hard it feels the glass could shatter. Wind whipping through the water. And the smell of the Earth, it was distinct. After the rain.” “Did you play in the rain?” “Lily told me the rain turned your skin blue.” Mira laughs softly. “No, your skin doesn’t turn blue. And, sometimes, we would get to play. But, mostly, my Mom used to say I’d catch a cold if I did.” “Is the water cold?” “No, it’s hot, silly!”

Clara Finch was kneading her bun dough one frosty December morning in Willowwick when she found a silver button. The button bore the Bellweather Manor crest, the home of Lord Bellweather who had disappeared three winters ago and hadn’t been heard from since. “Milo, come over here for a second,” Clara said. Her assistant Milo walked up. “Did anyone access the pantry this dough was stored in?” she asked. “I don’t think so. After all, the pantry is locked, and only you, me, and Aunt Dottie have access to it,” Milo said. “Then how do you think this silver button with the Bellweather crest got into it?” Milo gasped. Through the open door, a couple customer’s voices floated in.

As Captain Mara Vey’s starship plunged into deep space, the imperial sun was dying. Mara had never expected to hear from her lost brother again. Yet, just hours ago, she’d received a garbled transmission where he urged her to bring the crystal she stole from the tomb of Emperor Solen to a mysterious location that rerouted her mission into forbidden space. Their only source of navigation was the pulsing crystal. Mara frowned at it. I shouldn’t have stolen it, she thought, even though it did whisper my name. “Are you ever going to sleep, Captain?” Mara turned around, startled. Celeste had snuck up on her, again.

It happened again. At exactly 3:17am, all the traffic lights in the city blinked blue for a single second. Mara Venn had noticed it for the first time several months ago, as she did municipal tech repairs beneath Central Station. She still wasn’t sure if she was imagining it. ORISON ran all of the city’s infrastructure but it was highly regulated. Was there a hole in the security? Mara was sure that whatever it was, the regular blue flicker was not an accident. That’s why she had been carefully tracking the source of the signal across forgotten underground tunnels for weeks. The signal never disrupted the city’s systems.

Mira placed her head on her hands and looked out her window. The village was quiet and peaceful beneath the moonlight. “How strange it is, that all the sounds during the day disappear as the sun sets,” Mira wondered aloud. “Where do they go?” A moth landed on her window sill and Mira smiled at it. It tapped its legs against the window so Mira cracked it open a bit. “Thank you Mira!” the moth said, jumping inside. Mira yelped and jumped away. “Oh I’m sorry I didn’t mean to scare you,” the moth said.

When Mara woke up on her seventeenth birthday, her mirror was completely black and the king’s riders had been sent on a hunt across the city to search for the prophesied lost heir to the crown. Mara dressed quickly, wearing a high collared shirt as she always did to hide the tattoo beneath her collarbone. It was her only confirmation that she was the lost heir. The king’s riders were unlikely to search for her, an apprentice mapmaker. There was a tap on her window and Mara opened it to let Tavin in. “I’ve come bearing gifts,” Tavin announced. He laid out bags packed with food and money as well as some rusting swords. “Where did you get these?” Mara asked.

Julian Hart, the devilishly handsome Earl of Ashcombe, always stood out, even among the high society of the London Season’s ball. Eleanor tried to avoid his gaze as she quickly hid the letter from her late father in her small reticule. Her father had warned her to stay away from Julian, saying his easy smile only concealed evil thoughts. “Miss Vale, would you do me the honor of joining me on the next waltz?” Julian said. “I am sorry Mr. Hart, but my dance card is full,” Eleanor said with a sniff. Before she could object, Julian reached for her wrist and examined the dance card hanging from it. “There seems to be plenty of room on this Miss Vale,” he said.

In FeatherVille, Elena is the proud wonder of a bakery. Featherville is a small seaside town on an island, where magic is still alive but hasn’t been seen as strongly as it once was in the sleepy town. Every morning, Elena wakes up early every day to sweep the floor before her grandson Tomas wakes up because every morning features magically appear. She doesn’t want Tomas to have to worry about magic since he is still young so would rather him not find the feathers. After sweeping, she places the feathers in a special jar hidden in a cabinet up high where Tomas can’t reach. Tomas wakes up early for breakfast. He is nine years old and a magic skeptic.

When the alarm went off, Gerald was still half-asleep. Yet he realized something unusual had happened. His left shoe had started walking on the floor of his bedroom! “Thank you. Thank you. It is my honor to be elected as the Mayor of Footwear in this house. I will focus on improving the standard of living for all footwear, including sneakers, boots, sandals ……” The left shoe was giving a victory speech but was quickly interrupted by the right shoe. “The election was stolen from us!” His right shoe shouted, surrounded by a few slippers of Gerald. Apparently, they had organized themselves into a rivalry party.

Boone Biggerstaff was well-known far and wide for his canoe-sized boots, wide brimmed hat, and Kansas-rattling laugh. Despite his intimidating stature, he was a gentle giant and the best rancher in Dustpan County. Boone also had a way of fixing things. One brutal summer, Dustpan County experienced the most brutal drought recorded. All the water sources dried up and the mayor gathered all the remaining water from the town’s ponds and kept it guarded in his horse. Boone’s hens were so parched that they laid hard boiled eggs. Boone then decided that enough was enough. He was going to bring back the rain. His first step was to collect all the local lariats in the county.

You have one task. One task to complete before dawn. You have the brass key, you just need to find the door. You heard it’s hidden under the river, but it will take some time getting there. Where’s the river? Where are you? The world tilts a little. There’s a bell tolling just above you. You must be under the tower, which is…it’s difficult to recall how far the tower is from the river. You stagger forward and reach water. The river! No, not the river, just a fountain. Disappointment floods you. People around you seem to scatter fearfully, but what are they running from? You see them headed inside, maybe you should too. But, you made a promise.

While everyone else slept, Elian, an apprentice cartographer, sat looking at his map by the faint light of the green moon. He couldn't sleep, troubled by an uneasy feeling he couldn't explain. At that moment, a bell rang out with an extraordinary clarity that was nonetheless ominous. A sound unlike anything he ever had heard in his life. Anyone who heard it knew at least one thing - No human could have produced that sound, but only a supernatural power could have made it. It spread throughout the kingdom of Aerath and stirred unease among the people, who wondered why the bell had rung and what it foretold.

Vale was a valley of people whose most valued virtue was honesty. As a display of faith, each citizen carried a lantern with them always. Its blue flame was kept bright and alive by the people’s honesty. The light was so bright, travelers passing through the valley used it to guide them through the dark. But one day, a sniveling merchant named Sable began selling mirrors to anyone who would buy one. Mirrors were an enchanting novelty. People couldn’t stop gazing at themselves and admiring their image. They began lying to themselves to keep the image they saw in the mirror pristine. With time, their lanterns began to lose their glow.

There once was a girl who was destined to heal the Moon. She was discovered in a fire, unburned. Some said she was blessed, others cursed. They all knew she had a role to play in the fate of Tallow, their village. Why else would they find an infant in the ashes? On Ash’s seventeenth birthday, a lunar anomaly occurred. At first, it appeared as though the moon were growing bigger. But, then, the moon fractured into pieces. Sorcery. Darkness. Death. The tides were pulled back, the rivers flowed upwards, some plants were uprooted. It caused a very large disturbance. Ash watched as the water in her well rose up.

None of this is really my fault. I was born to be a rascal. My Ma gave birth to me under a tavern table while my Pa argued over dice. Ma and Pa didn’t have a big imagination, and I reckon that they decided to name me Christian during my christening and not one second earlier. Pa was in debt and, when he died, I inherited it. Such is the way of the world. At 16, I found a cushy job working with Baron Vellum. I was in charge of his hounds. He was obsessed with them. He’d order me to spoil the dogs and then yelled at me when his hunting expeditions ended in failure. It was all worth it though because the Baron paid well. Unfortunately, we parted on poor terms.

Lower Puddle was a small town with two big problems: taxes and dragons. Technically, the two problems were related. And there was only one dragon. Destiny led Sir Cedric the Moderately Brave to Lower Puddly one fine morning. Knowing the town needed a brave, courageous knight in shining armor, he had seized the opportunity and arrived by dawn. He was going to fight the tax-dragon. Cedric rode into town to be greeted by a circle of villagers holding makeshift weapons – a lamp, flower pots, and even an umbrella. “Oh, brave knight, you have come to free us all from this nightmare!” The crowd parted aside as a short, portly man waddled through.
